Chorin
kho-REEN
n. (the Brandenburg Cistercian abbey of 1273, a masterpiece of north German brick Gothic, now a roofless ruin)
German Chorin, from a Slavic place-name, perhaps chor, a thicket.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Chorin north-east of Berlin was founded in 1273 when the Cistercians of Mariensee moved to a better site, and the church they raised there is the finest brick Gothic building of the north German plain: a west front of tall blind arcading and slender turrets built entirely without stone, since the march had no quarries and the monks had clay. It was the Ascanian mausoleum until the line failed. The abbey was dissolved in 1542, served as a farm and a sawmill, lost its roof, and was rescued in the nineteenth century as a Romantic ruin, which is how it stands: walls and tracery open to the sky. The dictionary records Chorin among the ruins because Scripture treats a desolate sanctuary as a thing to mourn and to learn from rather than to admire. The lament over an emptied house is bitter, “The ways of Zion do mourn, because none come to the solemn feasts” (Lam 1:4), and the psalmist's complaint over a wrecked holy place is a complaint and not an aesthetic, “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary” (Psa 74:7). Micah was given to say that even the temple mount would become woodland, “the mountain of the house as the high places of the forest” (Mic 3:12). The hope held out is rebuilding and not picturesque decay, “they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations” (Isa 61:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a ruin as the remains of a decayed building; desolation as destruction, a place wasted; tracery as ornamental stonework in a window; Gothic as pertaining to the pointed style of architecture; and a mausoleum as a magnificent tomb.

expand to see more

RUIN, n. Destruction; fall; overthrow; also, the remains of a decayed or demolished city or house.

DESOLATION, n. The act of deserting or laying waste; a place deserted or laid waste; gloominess; sadness.

TRACERY, n. In architecture, ornamental stone-work, as in the heads of Gothic windows.

GOTHIC, adj. Pertaining to the Goths; denoting the style of architecture with pointed arches.

MAUSOLEUM, n. A magnificent tomb, or stately monument for the dead.

Key Scripture

Lam 1:4 — "The ways of Zion do mourn, because none come to the solemn feasts: all her gates are desolate: her priests sigh, her virgins are afflicted, and she is in bitterness."

Psa 74:7 — "They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground."

Mic 3:12 — "Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of the forest."

Isa 61:4 — "And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations."

Modern Corruption

Brandenburg Cistercian abbey of 1273, the finest brick Gothic church of the north, dissolved 1542 and kept as a roofless ruin.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a ruined house of worship is an occasion for mourning, not for taste. Chorin was saved in the nineteenth century because it looked well without a roof, and the scriptural register for an emptied sanctuary is grief, “all her gates are desolate” (Lam 1:4).

The live temptation is the picturesque, which turns judgment into scenery. The psalmist will not do it; he reports the wreck as an outrage, “they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground” (Psa 74:7). Micah was given to say the same of the temple itself, “Zion for your sake be plowed as a field” (Mic 3:12), and the promise attached to such places is labour and not admiration, “they shall raise up the former desolations” (Isa 61:4).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew abal (H0056), to mourn; Hebrew shamem (H8074), to be desolate; Hebrew miqdash (H4720), a sanctuary; Hebrew churbah (H2723), a waste, a ruin.

expand to see more

Hebrew abal (H0056) — to mourn, to lament; “The ways of Zion do mourn”, Lamentations 1:4.

Hebrew shamem (H8074) — to be desolate, to be laid waste; “all her gates are desolate”, Lamentations 1:4.

Hebrew miqdash (H4720) — a sanctuary, a holy place; “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary”, Psalm 74:7.

Hebrew bamah (H1116) — a high place; “as the high places of the forest”, Micah 3:12.

Hebrew churbah (H2723) — a waste place, a ruin; “they shall build the old wastes”, Isaiah 61:4.

Usage

"“The ways of Zion do mourn” (Lam 1:4) — the right register for an empty church."

"“They have cast fire into thy sanctuary” (Psa 74:7) — a wreck reported as an outrage."

"“they shall repair the waste cities” (Isa 61:4) — the promise is rebuilding, not scenery."
